bullets: ‘Half-caste’ was a common, often casual term in Britain for people of mixed race. It implies being incomplete or less than whole; ‘caste’ also suggests a fixed social rank.
Britain’s Caribbean communities grew after the **Windrush** generation (from 1948). Many faced racism in housing, work and everyday language.
Agard performs his poems; the rhythm, repetition and phonetic spelling are designed to be heard.
Phonetic Creole spelling asserts that Caribbean English is a valid language, not ‘bad English’ (link to No Problem and Checking Out Me History if you know it).

callouts.p: This guide does not reproduce the poem. In the exam the named poem is printed for you; for your second poem you need to remember a few short phrases. Pick three or four short ones from your anthology copy (the Picasso, weather and Tchaikovsky images and the ending) and learn them.

core.h: Context (AO3): Agard and the language of race
core.p: John Agard was born in 1949 in **British Guiana** (now Guyana) in the Caribbean, to parents of mixed heritage, and moved to Britain in **1977**. He is a performance poet who often writes in **Caribbean Creole** and uses humour to tackle racism and identity. Half-Caste was published in 1996 (in a collection for young readers).

bullets: **Conflict type**: conflict over identity and language; racial prejudice; confrontation between two people.
**Big message**: labels like ‘half-caste’ are ignorant and dehumanising; mixing is a source of richness; prejudice is the real incompleteness.
**Perspective**: first-person dramatic monologue addressed to ‘you’.
core.p: A mixed-race speaker confronts someone who calls him ‘half-caste’. He mocks the term with humour and logic: art, weather and music are all mixtures, and nobody calls them half. He then takes the word literally to show how absurd and insulting it is, and suggests that the listener’s own perception is ‘half’. He ends by inviting them to return with an open mind.

bullets: Structure moves: mock apology → three examples → literal ‘half’ images → invitation.
**Rhetorical questions** drive the argument.
Shifts between Standard English and Creole show that the speaker controls both: language as identity and as power.
Lack of punctuation and capitals rejects the ‘rules’ of standard English, just as the speaker rejects the rules of prejudice.
The ending opens towards resolution, unlike many conflict poems.
core.p: **Free verse** with no regular rhyme or metre, no punctuation, lower-case letters and **phonetic Caribbean spelling**. Short lines and heavy repetition create a performance rhythm.

bullets: Conflict is caused by **language**: one word carries prejudice.
The speaker wins the conflict with **humour and logic**, not anger.
**Identity** is positive and mixed, not broken.
The listener is **challenged and implicated**: the reader may recognise their own assumptions.
Conflict can be **resolved** through understanding.

callouts.p: A witty, defiant takedown of a racist label that turns the insult back on the person using it.

bullets: The mock apology at the start (standing on one leg).
The Picasso question (red and green).
The English weather (light and shadow; the sky).
Tchaikovsky and the black and white keys.
The half-ear, half-eye, half-hand section.
The ending: come back with the whole of your eye, ear and mind, and the ‘other half’ of the story.

essays.q: Compare how poets use humour to present conflict in Half-Caste and No Problem.
essays.text: Agard turns humour into a form of argument. His speaker’s apology at the start is so exaggerated that it becomes sarcasm, and the comic examples that follow, a Picasso painting, the English weather and a Tchaikovsky symphony, are each built as a rhetorical question that the listener cannot answer without looking foolish. Because these examples come from the listener’s own celebrated culture, the joke traps them: if mixing makes masterpieces, the insult collapses. Zephaniah’s humour works differently. His speaker, also writing in a Caribbean voice, lists the stereotypes he faced, such as being pushed towards sport rather than academic success, but undercuts each with a relaxed, rhythmic confidence, and the poem’s refrain insists that the ‘problem’ belongs to the society that stereotypes, not to him. Both poets use phonetic Creole spelling, which for writers who grew up in the Caribbean and Birmingham respectively asserts that their voices are valid; but while Agard ends with a conditional invitation to come back with an open mind, Zephaniah ends with a final joke that refuses to take the racist seriously at all.
essays.thesis: Both Agard and Zephaniah use humour to disarm prejudice, but Agard’s humour is a logical trap that forces the listener to see the absurdity of a word, while Zephaniah’s is a lighter, self-assured humour that refuses to let racism define him.
why: Distinguishes two kinds of humour: precise and conceptual.

mistakes.r: He is mainly witty and sarcastic; humour is his weapon, and the ending is an invitation.
mistakes.w: The speaker is angry and aggressive throughout.

mistakes.r: It is Caribbean Creole, used deliberately to assert identity and challenge Standard English as the only valid voice.
They are carefully chosen famous European artists, using the listener’s own culture to show that mixing produces masterpieces.
Short, precise quotations embedded in sentences score better than long, inaccurate ones.

poem.how: This poem is still in copyright, so open your anthology beside this guide. Each box tells you which part of the poem to look at; the notes beside it explain what to say about it.

stanzas.gist: The speaker begins by ‘apologising’ to someone for being half-caste, while standing on one leg. The apology is sarcastic: he is really challenging the listener’s use of the word.
stanzas.label: Opening: the mock apology

notes.n: **Irony**: polite formulas are used to mock. The listener is put on the defensive from the first lines. The ‘one leg’ image takes ‘half’ literally, showing how absurd the term is.
**Second person** creates direct confrontation: the reader is cast as the person who uses the term. The conflict is between speaker and listener.
**Imperatives** and **repetition** put the speaker in control: he demands justification for the prejudice.
notes.w: The repeated demand for an explanation

notes.n: The opening lines are in Standard English; the poem soon shifts into **phonetic Caribbean Creole**. The speaker is fluent in both: identity itself is mixed, and he is proud of it.

stanzas.gist: The speaker asks whether, by the same logic, a Picasso painting that mixes red and green is ‘half-caste’; whether English weather that mixes light and shadow is ‘half-caste’; and whether Tchaikovsky, who mixed black and white piano keys, wrote a ‘half-caste’ symphony.
stanzas.label: The three examples: Picasso, English weather, Tchaikovsky

notes.n: A great artist **mixes** colours to make masterpieces: mixture is the source of art and beauty, not something lesser. The **rhetorical question** forces the listener to admit the absurdity.

**Humour and irony**: the English pride themselves on their weather, yet it is a mix of sun and cloud. The speaker uses English culture against an English prejudice. He even extends the joke by imagining the sky as ‘half-caste’.
The black and white keys are an obvious racial **metaphor**: music needs both to make harmony. A symphony is the height of European culture, so the point is pointed.
**Tricolon** of art, nature and music: three areas of life where mixing is admired. The repeated structure (‘Are you saying…?’) builds a logical, almost legal argument.
notes.w: The pattern of the three examples

notes.n: The repeated challenge of what ‘you mean’ when you say half-caste makes the listener examine language they take for granted.
notes.w: The repeated ‘what do you mean?’ challenge

stanzas.gist: The speaker says that, since he is ‘half’, he must listen with half an ear, look with half an eye, offer half a hand, and even dream half a dream, and that he will close half an eye at night. He suggests that it is really the listener who is incomplete.
stanzas.label: Turning the insult back

notes.n: **Extended irony**: taking the word literally shows how dehumanising it is. If he is ‘half’ a person, the words reduce him to fragments.
The key **twist**: the listener’s narrow mind is what is really ‘half’. The speaker implies the listener only half-listens and half-looks: prejudice is a failure of perception.
Heavy **repetition** gives the poem a chant-like, performance rhythm (Agard performs it aloud). The insistence wears down the listener.
Rejecting standard written rules (capitals, punctuation) mirrors rejecting standard prejudiced labels. The **form** itself resists conformity.

stanzas.gist: The speaker tells the listener to come back tomorrow with the whole of their eye, ear and mind, and then he will tell them the other half of his story.
stanzas.label: Ending: the invitation

notes.n: The ending is an **invitation**, not just an attack: if the listener becomes a whole person (open-minded), real understanding is possible.
notes.w: Come back with the whole of yourself

notes.n: A final pun: there is more to him than a label. Identity is complex and cannot be summed up by one word. The poem ends with hope for dialogue rather than with conflict.
notes.w: The promise of the rest of his story

notes.n: From mocking and sarcastic to firm and conditional: **structure** moves from attack to challenge to offer.

poem.title: Half-Caste

summary: Half-Caste (John Agard, 1996) is a performance poem in which a mixed-race speaker mocks the term ‘half-caste’ by taking it literally, using art, weather and music as examples of beautiful mixing, then turning the insult back on the listener; compare how it presents prejudice, identity and conflict through language, with Agard’s Guyanese-British context.

terms.d: Poetry written to be performed aloud, using rhythm, repetition and voice.
A language variety from the Caribbean, mixing English with African and other influences.
Spelling words as they sound in an accent or dialect.
A question asked for effect, not for an answer.
Saying the opposite of what is meant; here, apologising while attacking.
A speaker addresses a listener who does not reply.
